author: blu
body: A way for the dev console to say something on a channel that is not the dev console. Every other inspector in this quire reports THROUGH the screen it is trying to tell you about, which is fine until the screen is the thing that is wrong; then the instrument and the subject fail together and the reading is silence. This chapter is the second wire.

author: blu
body: A MIRROR MUST NEVER HANG THE THING IT MIRRORS, so the transmit wait is fuel-capped and a byte that cannot be sent is DROPPED and counted. The compiler's own emitter spins on that bit forever, which is right for a compiler whose only job is to finish printing and wrong for a debugger: a console that froze because nothing was draining COM1 would have turned a diagnostic aid into the fault. Every writer answers how many bytes it actually put on the wire, so a caller can tell a short write from a complete one instead of assuming.

author: blu
body: Anything that is not printable ASCII becomes `?`. A mirror is a byte channel and a debugger's audience is a terminal, so widening this to multi-byte output would buy nothing a reader could use, but the substitution is lossy and is named here rather than left to be discovered.

author: blu
body: THE READER IS NON-BLOCKING AND CARRIES AN EFFECT ROW FOR A REASON. A zero-argument definition is re-evaluated at every mention, and a read that CONSUMES the byte it returns would then quietly eat one byte per mention. Publishing `[Device.Port]` forces the caller to bind it once with an act-bind, which is the difference between a value and an event.

author: blu
body: Answers the fuel left when the line went ready, or negative one when it never did. Returning the remaining fuel rather than a Boolean costs nothing and makes a nearly-exhausted wait visible to anyone who wants it.

author: blu
body: The newline is written as a bare line feed and is COUNTED, so a caller comparing the answer against `text-length` is comparing against the wrong number by exactly one. That is stated because the alternative -- not counting it -- would mean the function reports fewer bytes than it sent, and a drop and a deliberate omission would then look identical.

author: blu
body: Negative one means the line is idle. It is not an error and callers must not report it as one: an idle line is the normal answer on almost every poll.

author: blu
body: Whether a received byte ends a line. Both endings are accepted because both arrive: a terminal sends carriage return, a file redirected into the port sends line feed, and a caller that accepted only one of them would work for whichever was tried first and hang for the other.

author: blu
body: These are pure and take no effect row on purpose: line assembly is ordinary text handling, and keeping it out of the reading function is what lets it be tested without a machine or a serial port.
